https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.text: Image source, X/Reuters Image caption, The islands of Amami and Okinawa are the parts of Japan most affected by the typhoon By Jack Burgess Published 3 hours ago Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday. Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived. The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes. Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival. The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country. Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Satellite imagery showing Typhoon Dolphin approaching Japan's Okinawa during the week In China, Zhejiang's Ningbo Lishe International Airport said it would stop its operations from 23:30 local time on Saturday (15:30 GMT) and suspend all flights on Sunday. A coastal typhoon alert in Zhejiang has been raised to its highest level, and port and ferry services have been halted in the Chinese province. Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. This year is a strong El NiÃ±o year , which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense. In an average year of 25 cyclones reaching tropical storm strength in the region, around three usually make landfall in Japan, according to the country's meteorological agency. Some of these will be strong enough to be classified as typhoons â as was the case with Dolphin. A typhoon is the term used for storms that form in the north-west Pacific, whereas a hurricane is the term used for storms that form in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrk.text: Image source, US Department of Homeland Security By Madeline Halpert Published 4 hours ago Immigrants held at "Alligator Alcatraz", a now-shuttered detention centre in Florida, were kept in small metal cages for hours, according to a report from the US Department of Homeland Security's watchdog. The Office of the Inspector General (OIG) found the use of the outdoor cages - about 18sq ft (1.67sq m) - was "unprecedented among detention facilities" and dangerous. Investigators concluded the centre also did not comply with a number of standards for hygiene, medical care, food, health and safety. The BBC has contacted DHS's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis for comment. DHS told the watchdog that state officials ran the facility. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Trump toured the Alligator Alcatraz facility last July In its response included in the investigation report, DHS officials said Florida - not the federal government - had authority over day-to-day operations at the facility. The facility was established by the state of Florida through an executive order signed by DeSantis, but the federal government paid for operational costs. In January, the OIG conducted a surprise inspection at the detention facility, which had become one of the most notorious immigration detention centres in the US. The OIG is an independent internal watchdog at DHS. The current inspector general was appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term. In 2025, the detention facility was built over the course of eight days in the Everglades, a protected wetland known for its alligators. Trump once joked that immigrants held there would need to learn "how to run away" from the reptiles at the facility, which civil rights groups have decried as inhumane. In June 2026, DeSantis said the facility would close as it was only meant to be temporary. According to the OIG report, between July 2025 and January 2026, the facility kept 79 immigrants in the small metal enclosures, describing them as "calming areas" for people to "deescalate and have time alone". They were held there from periods ranging from minutes to nearly two hours, at least once as a disciplinary measure, OIG said. "The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment," the report stated. Figure caption, Watch: âI have grave concernsâ - Advocate weighs environmental impact of âAlligator Alcatraz" Detainees at the facility have previously told the BBC they were denied necessary medication and regular showers and other hygiene measures. In their report, OIG inspectors said they found immigrants held at the facility had to use showers infested with small bugs and were only allowed to do so three times a week. The facility did not provide them with sufficient living space, "creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units", according to the report. Immigrants at the centre also told OIG that they did not have access to clean drinking water and could not clean the plastic cups from which they drank. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60r.text: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospital By James FitzGerald Published 8 October 2026 Christa Pike is "up and walking" though mentally "foggy" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her legal team says. Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented. Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but had learned her arms were swollen and barely functioning as she took her first steps around her hospital room. A court has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state. The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection. The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death. Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison. Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people. How did Christa Pike survive two lethal injections? Published 17 hours ago What happens next in the Pike case? Published 18 hours ago In their previous updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed. Her lawyer Randy Spivey said after Wednesday's court hearing: "She cannot move either of her arms." He added: "Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what if any function she will regain in her arms." In the later updates, given on Wednesday to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital. The drug was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September. But once it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the execution attempt, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to be in a critical condition. As of late on Wednesday, though, Pike was "fairly well", Ferrell said. "What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much." Of her physical movements, Ferrell added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far." Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going." Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet." He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now". Image source, Family handout Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach. They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole. Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair." Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know. For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution. Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt. The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels. The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt. She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case. Correction 8 October: This article originally said that Pike and her boyfriend had first met Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp for "troubled teens".
